questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, $n$ bidders submit bids $b_i\ge0$ simultaneously and the highest bid wins. If bidder $i$ wins, how much does she pay?
options: Her own bid $b_i$, the highest bid submitted
The second-highest valuation among all $n$ bidders
The highest bid among the other bidders, $\max_{j\ne i}b_j$
The average of the bids submitted by the other bidders

questions.question: A bidder with private value $\theta_i$ takes part in a second-price sealed-bid auction; let $c=\max_{j\ne i}b_j$ be the highest rival bid. What does her own bid $b_i$ determine?
options: Both whether she wins and how much she pays
Only the price she pays, since the winner is drawn at random
Only whether she wins, since the price she pays is $c$
How much the losing bidders have to pay

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with private values, bidding one's value $b_i=\theta_i$ is weakly dominant. Why is it not strictly dominant?
options: Against many rival bids, other bids give exactly the same payoff
Against some rival bids, overbidding gives a strictly higher payoff
Truthful bidding is a best response only to truthful rival bids
Strict dominance requires the bidder to know the rivals' values

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction a bidder with private value $\theta_i$ bids $b_i>\theta_i$; let $c$ be the highest rival bid. In which case does this overbid change her outcome compared with bidding $\theta_i$, and how?
options: When $c<\theta_i$: she now pays more than she would have paid
When $c>b_i$: she now wins although a rival bid more
When $\theta_i<c<b_i$: she now wins and gains $b_i-c$
When $\theta_i<c<b_i$: she now wins but pays $c>\theta_i$, a loss

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values drawn from a distribution $F$, the truthful profile $b_i(\theta_i)=\theta_i$ is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium. For which distributions $F$ does this hold?
options: Only for uniform distributions, which make the rivals' bids predictable
Only for symmetric $F$, so that all bidders face the same rivals
Only when $F$ is common knowledge among the bidders
For every distribution $F$, as no beliefs about rivals are used

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction a bidder values the object at $10$ and bids $12$; the highest rival bid is $11$. What is her payoff?
Three bidders in a second-price sealed-bid auction submit bids $b_1=5$, $b_2=8$ and $b_3=6$. Bidder 2's private value is $9$. What is bidder 2's payoff?

In a second-price sealed-bid auction a bidder values the object at $10$ and compares bidding $8$ with bidding $10$. Ignoring exact ties, for which highest rival bids $c$ does bidding $8$ give a strictly lower payoff?
options: For $c<8$ only
For $c>10$ only
For every $c<10$
For $8<c<10$ only

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction a bidder with value $10$ bids $10$, and the highest rival bid is also exactly $10$; the tie is broken at random. What is her payoff, whichever way the tie is broken?

Two bidders have independent $U[0,1]$ private values and both bid truthfully in a second-price sealed-bid auction. Bidder 1 has value $0.7$, so she wins when $\theta_2<0.7$ and then pays $\theta_2$. What is her expected payoff?

In a first-price sealed-bid auction the winner pays her own bid; in a second-price one she pays the highest rival bid. With private values, why does the first-price auction have no weakly dominant bid while the second-price auction does?
options: In the first-price auction bidding one's value is weakly dominated by bidding above it
There the bid also sets the price, so the best bid depends on rival bids
In the first-price auction losers also pay their bids, which makes every bid risky
In the first-price auction bidders do not know their own values when they bid

questions.question: Two bidders have private values in $[0,1]$ in a second-price sealed-bid auction. The profile ‘bidder 1 always bids $1$, bidder 2 always bids $0$’ is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium. Which argument rules it out as a prediction?
options: It is not an equilibrium, because bidder 2 gains by bidding above $1$ when her value is high
Both bids are weakly dominated by truthful bids, so deleting such bids removes it
Both bids are strictly dominated, and no Nash equilibrium uses strictly dominated strategies
It requires each bidder to know the other's value, which private values rule out

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with $n\ge3$ bidders and private values, why does the two-bidder argument that bidding one's value is weakly dominant carry over unchanged?
options: Each bidder only needs to outbid one randomly chosen rival
Only the highest rival bid $c=\max_{j\ne i}b_j$ matters for her payoff
With more bidders the price approaches each bidder's own value
Rival bids are independent, so the bidder can treat them one by one

questions.question: Three bidders have independent $U[0,1]$ values and bid truthfully in a second-price sealed-bid auction. For bidder 1 with value $0.6$, the highest rival value $Y$ has density $2y$ on $[0,1]$; she pays $Y$ when $Y<0.6$. What is her expected payment?

Four bidders have i.i.d. $U[0,1]$ values and bid truthfully in a second-price sealed-bid auction. Using $\mathbb{E}[\theta_{(k)}]=\frac{k}{n+1}$ for the $k$th smallest of $n$ uniform values, what is the seller's expected revenue?

Two bidders have independent $U[0,1]$ values in a second-price sealed-bid auction, and bidder 2 bids truthfully. Bidder 1 has value $0.7$. By how much does her expected payoff change if she bids $0.9$ instead of $0.7$?
options: It falls by $0.20$
It falls by $0.04$
It falls by $0.02$
It is unchanged

questions.question: Suppose the object is worth the same unknown amount to every bidder, and each bidder only observes a private noisy signal of it before a second-price sealed-bid auction. Why does the argument that bidding one's estimate is weakly dominant break down?
options: A rival's bid carries information about one's own value of the object
The winner then pays her own bid rather than the highest rival bid
The argument needs values drawn from a uniform distribution
Truthful bidding is only dominant when bidders' values differ

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with ties broken at random, bidder 1 has value $10$ and may bid any $b\ge0$, while the only bids available to her single rival are $0$ and $20$. Is bidding $10$ a weakly dominant strategy for bidder 1?
options: Yes: bidding one's value is weakly dominant in every second-price auction
Yes, and even strictly dominant, as no rival bid lies between $10$ and $12$
No: bids such as $12$ give the same payoff against both rival bids
No: bidding $20$ does strictly better against the rival bid $20$

questions.question: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with ties broken at random, a bidder with value $10$ knows for certain that the highest rival bid will be $15$. Which bids are best responses for her?
options: Every bid below $15$, including her value $10$
Only the bid $10$, her weakly dominant strategy
Only bids at most $10$, as bidding above one's value is never optimal
Only the bid $0$, since she is certain to lose anyway

questions.question: Two bidders have independent $U[0,1]$ values in a second-price sealed-bid auction and play the equilibrium in which bidder 1 always bids $1$ and bidder 2 always bids $0$. Which pair gives the seller's expected revenue and then the probability that the lower-value bidder gets the object?
